query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored slow cooling heat‐treatment after solution homogenization will produce serrated grain boundaries in (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38, thereby increasing its toughness and load‐bearing integrity without degrading its intrinsic field‐ and pressure‐induced caloric performance.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 produced by conventional melting/casting procedures exhibits predominantly straight grain boundaries; while its caloric phase transformation is robust, its mechanical integrity is poor with tendencies to crack under load.
generation.intervention: After a high-temperature solution homogenization step (e.g., at ≈850–900 °C), subject the alloy to a controlled slow cooling process (e.g., 1–5 °C/min) rather than quenching. This controlled cooling is intended to promote the nucleation and coarsening of secondary precipitates along the grain boundaries, which interact with moving boundaries to produce a serrated (undulated) morphology.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be performed under inert or controlled atmosphere following homogenization. Subsequent performance evaluations are to be made under the operational field (magnetic/pressure) and temperature ranges at which the caloric effect is normally activated (for example, room temperature to moderate temperatures) and under the modest mechanical loads expected in refrigeration applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of serrated grain boundaries mediated by coarse precipitates, which interrupts the continuity of brittle, straight boundaries and blunts stress concentration sites.
generation.mechanism: The serpentine (undulated) boundary morphology distributes local strain more evenly and impedes crack nucleation and propagation. Because this post-processing only alters the microstructural morphology without substantially changing the chemical composition or the phase transitions responsible for the caloric effect, the caloric response under applied field/pressure is largely preserved.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unchanged alloy it is predicted that the slow-cooled variant will exhibit significantly improved fracture toughness (higher ductility and longer creep rupture life) while retaining a caloric response (adiabatic temperature/entropy change) comparable to that of the original material.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or conventionally quenched (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which shows excellent caloric response but suffers from poor load-bearing integrity due to straight, brittle grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: The improved properties are expected to be maintained under typical refrigeration operating conditions – applied magnetic and/or pressure fields at ambient to moderate temperatures and under mechanical loads corresponding to service conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While studies such as PMC9848264 (demonstrating the effectiveness of serrated grain boundaries in enhancing ductility) and PMC6353877 (illustrating the benefits of heterogeneous microstructures) support the mechanical benefits of such interventions, it is uncertain how a slow cooling regime might subtly affect the phase transformation kinetics underlying the caloric effect in (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples: one set processed with the standard quench (yielding straight grain boundaries) and a second set subjected to the slow cooling heat treatment as described. Characterize the grain boundary morphologies (via electron microscopy), measure mechanical properties (fracture toughness, tensile ductility, creep life) and assess the caloric performance (e.g., adiabatic temperature change or isothermal entropy change under applied-field and pressure cycles) under identical test conditions.
measurements: Electron microscopy images to confirm serrated vs. straight grain boundaries
Fracture toughness and tensile strain-to-failure data
Creep rupture life under representative loading
Caloric response metrics (adiabatic temperature change and entropy change) under operating fields/pressures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow cooled (serrated boundary) samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., an increase of >20% in fracture toughness or ductility) while maintaining caloric performance within experimental uncertainty of the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
